blocks.text: Addendum.
The Silkworm.

First, by way of addendum, we give the explanation of a passage in Rashi in which the silkworm is mentioned. In Menachoth 39b and Sabbat 20b three kinds of silk are mentioned. The first is called שיראים, the Seric silk, which, as is well known, the Seric merchants, who traversed almost the entire breadth of Asia, brought in processed form to the fairs at Nisibis in ancient Mesopotamia (Voigt l. c. 5, p. 95).
The second is called סריקון; this is the silk [p. 359] that the caterpillar Noctua serici spins. This silk is not as serviceable as that of the Bombyx mori.

The third is called כלך, which is also called כילכא and גושקרא. On Sabbat Rashi explains: פסולת של משי העשוי ככובעים והוא בית החולעת וקורין לו פולוייל ונופצין איתו וטווהו ועושה ממנו בגד "The waste of the silk, in the shape of little caps; it is the casing of the caterpillar and is called פולוייל; one separates and spins it and makes garments from it."

The foreign word is miswritten here; in the first Rashi passage (Menachoth l. c.) it reads: פלוציל, i.e., Filoselle, floss or floret silk. For when spinning itself in, the caterpillar first weaves a raw web of coarser threads, from which floret silk is made, then the silk proper, which forms a thread of more than 900 feet in length, and finally the cocoon, a dense texture which is used for silk wadding, a more flocculent substance.

According to Rashi on the second passage, the three kinds of silk named appear to be made from those three aforementioned components of the web. שיראים is the silk proper, כלך the floret silk, and סיריקין the silk spun from the cocoon; Rashi says: סיריקין is the soft, divisible kind of silk found in the silk, which in our place is called יר"ש. The foreign word will probably read ירש, i.e. Vers, the silkworms. Yet I would not wish to assert this interpretation of Rashi as certain.
Difficult and in any case corrupt is the Rashi passage on Menachoth l. c. It reads: [הוא בית החולעה] כלך, מעיל שעושין מאותן דגים [ במינן שקורין פלוצ"יל שמצויין במינוי
A gloss already reads for במינוי.
For דגים one must undoubtedly read דקים, for also for the הרג occurring in Tos. ibid. s.v. בגד, the Tos. Sabbat 27a. s.v. ונוצה already correctly read: הרק.

For במינוי one should read במשי, as Rashi Sabbat 20b also has המצוי במשי, or else בנימין "in the threads", and if we omit the later bracketed addition entirely, Rashi means to say that כלך is silk prepared from the thin, i.e., not very solid and flocculent threads. Admittedly, it is precisely floret silk that is coarser] but it is not surprising that Rashi explains כלך differently here than at Sabbat l. c., since similar divergences in Rashi's explanations are not rare.

I here compile the zoological foreign words from the Shulchan Aruch and in part from Bet Josef. A compilation [p. 360] of most of the foreign words from the four Shulchan Aruch I gave in Frankel's Monatsschrift für Gesch. und Wissensch. d. Judenth. 1856, p. 441 ff. and p. 477 ff.

S. Ar. Jore Dea. Siman 28, Seif 4 בופלי, Büffel, buffalo. — 57, 3. פלקון, falcon. — 82 Bet Josef קורן, Spanish Corneja, crow.
אישפרויר, Épervier and גאוילן, Spanish Gavilan, sparrowhawk.
גולונדרינא, Spanish Golondrina, swallow.
סינואיניא, Spanish Ciguëña, stork.
אנולא, Spanish Aguila, eagle. — 83, 5 הערינג, Häring, herring.
מרקריש, perhaps the French Maguereau, the small mackerel.

In Sota 42b it is said: The giant Goliath was בר מאה כפי וחרא "the son of a hundred כפי and one נאנאי." The word נאנאי כפי Rashi explains by פרשט"רא, more correctly in Ain Jacob: פרש"טרוש, i.e. Pédérastes, pederasts, and נאנאי by: father; the sense is: the mother of that giant was a venal person; she gave herself to many (a hundred is an indefinite round number; see Rashi) libertines, even to the pederasts who are otherwise contemptuous of women; only one was the actual father of the giant. Buxdorf (Lex. p. 1350) did not understand this passage and translates כפי by Pape as a proper name. (A compilation of the most striking errors in the work of this lexicographer I shall give in Kobak's Jeschurun.) The glossator on Jalk. Schimoni part 2, fol. 17, d explains the word נאנאי differently, namely by כלב, dog. The Tosephot (on the Talmud passage s.v. מאה) take the word in precisely this sense and justify it on the ground that Goliath said to David: "Am I then a dog?" (1. Sam. 17, 43). I believe that the word, like the other names for the dog נבחן and למם (§. 122), is formed after a characteristic of the animal. The dog is called both in the Bible (Jes. 56, 11) and in the Talmud עז נפש, or עז פנים, the impudent, the unruly one, and so it may also have been called ἀνήνιον [anēnion] [p. 361]; the α [a] was lost, as in פנטי, equivalent to ἀπάντησις [apantēsis]; גמטא from ἄγασμα [agasma]; קרקע from ἀγκροικία [ankroikia] and פטטרכא from ἀπόπατος [apopatos]; see p. 38, note **.
The Stone Bumblebee.

In the Midrash (Rabba Kohelet fol. 82, col. c) it is said: צלן של דבורים שאין בו ממש של כלום "the shadow of the bees is almost completely imperceptible", to which Matnat Kehuna adds: I found in the work Ot Emet, in the name of Rashi, the explanation that the wings of the bees cast no shadow.

We should probably think here of a species belonging to the bee genus whose wings, because of their light colour, cast no perceptible shadow; thus the stone bumblebee (Bombus lapidarius) is black with a rust-red rear end and glass-clear on the wings (Voigt l. c. 4, p. 279).
